newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel-euro must match mark or Bonn not interested.
newsitem.headline: Waigel-euro must match mark or Bonn not interested.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Saturday the planned single European currency must be as stable as the mark or it will be of no interest to Germany.

Waigel told a local party meeting of his Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats, that the CSU must demonstrate unity ahead of the October 1998 general election which would be so tough that previous votes would seem like "dull training fights."
"But we will make it if we are united," Waigel said.
He said a stable euro, scheduled to be launched in 1999, would be a great opportunity for Bavaria and for Germany.
The planned European Central Bank (ECB) would be committed to monetary stability "and to no one else." It would carry on the work done by the Bundesbank in ensuring a stable currency.
The CSU has put itself at the centre of a fierce debate in Germany about how strictly the Maastricht Treaty's convergence criteria should be applied in order to ensure a stable euro.
Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, a leading CSU member, has insisted on the strictest possible interpretation of the criteria and said a delay of the project would be preferable to a soft currency.
He has argued that nations must not be allowed any leeway to let their deficits exceed the Maastricht ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

The debate centres on whether the somewhat vague wording of the treaty means a country must hit 3.0 on the nose, or whether a slight overshooting is allowed if mid-term financial planning shows a trend toward budget stability.
The issue caused such friction within Kohl's ruling coalition that Kohl last week committed himself to hitting the 3.0 percent level exactly.

Waigel on Friday secured government approval for a supplementary 1997 budget that he pledged would enable Germany to cut its deficit to 3.0 percent but independent economists continue to doubt whether Germany can make it.
